sistemas independientes de agua (SIAs), que son organizaciones sociales que suministran el servicio de agua a través de una red de infraestructura hídrica local autogestionada, y que se han provisto de normas operativas internas para su gestión. De acuerdo con la investigación de campo y datos del Sistema Administrador de Agua Potable y Alcantarillado de la Ciudad de Huajuapan de León (SAPAHUA, 2018), el gobierno municipal abastece a 88 localidades y los SIAs a 38, por lo que existen 27 localidades sin suministro continuo de agua.

En entrevistas con exintegrantes de los comités de agua de San Mateo y San Diego se evidenció que esta situación ya sucedió en sus localidades, donde entregaron el control de su SIA al gobierno municipal, y la cantidad y calidad del agua que reciben ahora es inferior a lo que les abastecía su propio sistema.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking water supply access (piped water connections and intermittent supply schedules) as well as municipal sewerage/drainage coverage across urban neighborhoods and rural municipal agencies in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines local institutional and legal water governance ('governance from below' via Independent Water Systems [SIAs] vs. the municipal water utility SAPAHUA and Mexico's Ley de Aguas Nacionales [LAN]). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it empirically analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access: (1) utility ownership and regulatory structure (community-owned, self-regulated SIAs operating under written and customary operational rules and Conagua concessions without formal recognition in the LAN, versus transfer of control to the municipal utility SAPAHUA); (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (flat monthly household tariffs vs. metered tiered pricing in Colonia del Maestro, plus extraordinary community assessments and tequios to cover pumping electricity deficits); (3) enforcement constraints on disconnection (non-paying users invoking the human right to water, preventing SIAs from cutting off service); and (4) land-tenure and jurisdictional service boundaries in peri-urban communal agrarian lands managed clandestinely as private property.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative comparative empirical study of four SIA case studies (two urban, two rural) using the Governance Analytical Framework (MAG), based on 20 in-depth key-informant interviews with water committee authorities, community actors, and municipal/SAPAHUA officials, triangulated with municipal utility and census records. Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple concrete service-access outcomes: household piped connection and sewerage counts, municipal coverage shares (70% SAPAHUA across 88 localities, 23% SIAs across 38 localities, 27 localities without continuous supply), service continuity/intermittency schedules (days and hours per week), monthly tariff levels and cost-recovery shortfalls, non-disconnection of non-paying households, exclusion/unserved peripheral growth by SIAs, and lower water quantity and quality following transfer of SIA control to the municipal operator.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (four SIA localities serving 1,200 to 5,200 inhabitants each, household connections, 20 key informants, and 153 municipal localities), exposure (community SIA ownership, internal operational/tariff/enforcement rules, and lack of LAN recognition vs. municipal utility control), outcomes (coverage, connection counts, continuity, tariffs, quantity/quality), and study design (qualitative multiple-case study) are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English abstract. Eligible under Inclusion Criterion 10 because translation from the clean, machine-readable Spanish full text is directly feasible and the study provides substantive empirical socio-legal evidence on community vs. municipal utility governance and access rules (translation method: bilingual/AI full-text reading, to be logged in extraction_note).

study_design: Qualitative comparative multiple-case study (4 cases; 20 in-depth key-informant interviews triangulated with municipal and census records, analyzed via the Governance Analytical Framework)
population_and_sample: Four Independent Water Systems (SIAs) in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico—two urban (Fraccionamiento Jardines del Sur, 1,200 inhabitants/146 piped dwellings; Colonia del Maestro, 5,200 inhabitants/651 piped dwellings) and two rural municipal agencies (Santa María Xochixtlapilco, 4,100 inhabitants/446 piped dwellings; Santa Teresa, 4,000 inhabitants/847 piped dwellings, 1,100 registered connections)—sampled via 20 in-depth key-informant interviews (16 SIA informants and 4 municipal/SAPAHUA officials) plus municipal data covering 153 localities (77,547 inhabitants).
exposure: Community-owned and user-regulated Independent Water Systems (SIAs) operating under written and customary local rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules (flat fees, metered block tariffs, extraordinary assessments, tequios), human-right-to-water non-disconnection constraints, and non-recognition under the Ley de Aguas Nacionales (LAN), compared with municipal utility (SAPAHUA) ownership/control and peri-urban agrarian tenure boundaries.
outcome: Household piped drinking-water connections and municipal coverage shares, intermittent supply continuity (days and hours per week), monthly household tariffs and system cost recovery, inability to disconnect non-paying users, peripheral coverage limits, and water quantity and perceived quality.
rationale: This qualitative socio-legal multiple-case study meets all review inclusion criteria. It empirically investigates household and community drinking-water access across four Independent Water Systems (SIAs) and the municipal utility (SAPAHUA) in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico, using 20 in-depth interviews and institutional records. Under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it examines concrete institutional and regulatory mechanisms directly governing service access: community vs. municipal utility ownership/regulatory control, lack of formal recognition under the Ley de Aguas Nacionales, local tariff and cost-recovery rules (flat vs. metered tiered tariffs and extraordinary community contributions), non-disconnection of non-paying users invoking the human right to water, operational rationing rules, and peri-urban agrarian land-tenure/jurisdictional boundaries. Although written in Spanish (with an English abstract), full-text translation is directly feasible under Criterion 10, and qualitative empirical studies are retained for mechanism synthesis.
